lead: Minnesota winters freeze pipes and build ice dams, and spring brings river floods. DryFlare helps owners from Minneapolis to Duluth get water out and get dry.
risk: frozen pipes, ice dams and spring river flooding
risk_short: frozen pipes, ice dams, river floods
why: Minnesota's cold is extreme. When temperatures stay well below zero, pipes freeze in outside walls, garages and cabins. Ice dams form on homes that lose heat into the attic, and meltwater runs into ceilings and walls. Spring melt then saturates the ground and seeps into basements.

River flooding hits in wet springs, especially along the Red River and the Minnesota River. In June 2012, heavy rain flooded Duluth and washed out streets. FEMA has declared 12 flood disasters in Minnesota since 2000. Neighbors North Dakota and Wisconsin share the same melt and freeze cycles.
image_alt: Water dripping from a frozen and split copper pipe
image_caption: A Minnesota cold snap can split pipes in garages and outside walls overnight.
problems: Older homes with attic heat loss
Red River valley and river towns
tips: Drain the water system at cabins you close for winter.
Add attic insulation and ventilation to reduce ice dams.
Clear snow away from the foundation before the spring thaw.
Keep the furnace serviced; a failed furnace freezes pipes fast.
insurance: Policies often cover sudden pipe bursts but exclude freeze damage when a home or cabin is left unheated, so read the vacancy terms.

faq.q: How do I thaw a frozen pipe safely in Minnesota?
faq.a: Open the nearest faucet and warm the pipe with a hair dryer, heat tape or space heater. Never use a torch or open flame. If the pipe has split, shut off the main water valve before it thaws and call for help.

licensing: The Minnesota Department of Labor and Industry licenses residential building contractors and remodelers. Check the license number before any rebuild.
